messages.subject: Handling Uncertainty/Measurement Error in Stan
parts:
I've generated some sample panel data with multivariate normal returns for 10 groups of 10 random variables each, such that there is correlation between groups but no correlation within groups (the only thing that is observed is the 100 random variables and which group they belong to). I then used Stan to perform cross-sectional regressions at each period of time to estimate the group means (this is an approach used in finance). The result of this is an array of the distribution of each group' returns in each period of time.

If I were Gibbs sampling, I could use these simulated distributions to estimate a mean or covariance matrix of the groups' returns. Alternately, I could do a time-series regression of each of the variables against their respect group. Alternately, I could subtract the original returns for the variables minus their respective groups and then perform any analysis on the residuals.

Would it be possible to handle the second part of the analysis in Stan as an alternative to Gibbs? There's a section on measurement error in the manual, but I already have information about how the measurement error for these variables presents itself. I don't need to simulate anything else.

In a Gibbs sampling approach, I can just add extra steps to each iteration that use the distributions I simulate during the Gibbs sampler.

More detail that may not be all that necessary:
I'm testing fitting some finance asset pricing models with Stan, particularly for use in portfolio management. There's a few papers out there that fit traditional asset pricing models with a hierarchical Bayesian approach, but they focus on the means and variances. The important thing for portfolio management is not just the means and variances, but also the correlations between different securities. Factor models are a common approach to dealing with the large number of correlations to be estimated.

If I fit a hierarchical model of the form:

y ~ N(a[s], sigma^2) where s is an indicator for industry and sigma is an idiosyncratic variance

then it will ignore the correlations. Alternately, a common factor model like:

y ~ N(a[s] + b * x_mkt, sigma^2) where x_mkt is the return on the market

is essentially using the aggregate to predict the underlying, which you have criticized on your blog. I can reformulate this in terms of a structured multivariate normal distribution, but it doesn't easily scale for more sophisticated distributions that are common in finance.

So my first step is to fit a cross-sectional factor model or fundamental factor model (it's from an old paper by Barr Rosenberg), which is a regression cross-sectionally in each period of time using the parameters of some factors. You do that each period in time and then the coefficients to that regression would be like the returns to different factors. You can then forecast the returns and use the factor return forecasts to generate forecasts for the stocks. So for instance, I might regress the stock returns for a period against the price earnings ratio for each stock and an indicator for each industry. The coefficients then represent the returns to a P/E factor and industry factors.

I've already done the above in Stan (excluding the P/E variable) using a hierarchical approach. The result is that each period there is a simulated distribution for the industry/factor return for that period.

Suppose I take the mean of the distribution of returns in each period. This is like treating factor returns like they are known, which means I can apply any type of analysis I want in Stan.The approach I'm using is like regressing

y ~ N(a[s] + b * x[s], sigma^2) where x[s] is the time series of industry returns

so that if you simulate from the posterior predictive of the x's, then the y's will be properly correlated. It's also bottom-up, avoiding the issue mentioned above. It's flexible in that I can separately fit the x's to incorporate things like time-varying means, variances, and fat tails only on the factors.

However, by assuming those are just returns instead of a distribution, I'm losing the information about the estimation error. I can incorporate them just fine in a Gibbs Sampling approach since I have the simulated returns in each iteration and can just add extra steps to perform any additional analysis. I'm just not sure if I can do it in Stan.

parts:
I'm also a little unclear on what the problem is.

Are you asking whether we can do cut like in BUGS?
The closest we can come is using the generated quantities
block to generate new variables based on fitted values.
It uses the parameters in each sample, so propagates that
uncertainty.

For example,

data {
int N;
real y[N];
int N_sim;
}
parameters {
real mu;
real<lower=0> sigma;
model {
y ~ normal(mu,sigma);
}
generated quantities {
real y_sim[N_sim];
for (n in 1:N_sim)
y_sim[n] ~ normal_rng(mu,sigma);
}

This fits the parameters mu and sigma based on the data
y, then generates M new variates y_sim. There's no feedback
from the generated quantities to the model. If you instead
declared y_sim as a parameter and included

y_sim ~ normal(mu,sigma);

in the model, then you do joint inference for (mu,sigma,y_sim).
In this case, I think the answers should be equivalent other than
that generated_quantities will be more efficient --- it shouldn't change
your inferences for mu and sigma.

You can't do anything with the posterior means directly in
Stan, because you can't express it as a log probability function.
You could, though, generate a fit, take the posterior means,
then plug that back in somewhere else.

Maybe if you wrote down a sketch of the BUGS model for what you're
trying to do, it would be easier for us to understand exactly
what you're trying to do.

- Bob

Yes, Stan requires you to write down the full probability
function as does any kind of full Bayesian modeling.

Your algorithm sketch doesn't look like a Gibbs sampler to me.
If you have N parameters theta[1],...,theta[N], and full probability
function p(theta[1],...,theta[N]), then Gibbs initializes theta, then
does

for (i in 1:I)
for (n in 1:N)
sample theta[n] from p(theta[n] | theta[1],..,theta[n-1],theta[n+1],...,theta[N])

I don't understand your estimate/simulate notation.

The short answer is that you can't mix simulation and sampling
in Stan. You can sample and do simulations based on the samples,
but you can't then feed the simulations back into the sampler in any way.

- Bob

You can do that in Stan using the generated quantities block.
The parameters are declared as parameters, the model is in
the model, then the quantities to generate conditional on
the parameters are declared and defined in the generated quantities
block.

This is one of the reasons we built the generated quantities --- to
generate predictive quantities based on the parameters.

If you do Gibbs, you have to have the joint probability anyway,
assuming your model's consistent --- the conditionals should
be conditionals of a joint probability. Technically, all you
need is something proportional to the posterior p(parameters|data),

Bayes's rule. Sorry if this is all obvious.

On Jan 27, 2014, at 5:41 PM, John Hall wrote:

I think I've stumbled across what I needed, albeit it's a little slow. A simple set of code is below (using just one index). This approach can be used for hierarchical models when you want to be able to model some kind of systematic factor and exposures to such a factor. My example was meant for an asset pricing model (in finance) that estimates a bottom-up market factor instead of using the observed market returns.

I generated some x's that are effectively the cross-sectional mean in each period of the y's. I then regress each of the y's against x. Importantly, I do this in two separate steps to ensure the x's will be tied down.

When I was originally trying to get this to work in one Stan file, I had tried this format, but crucially without the first y statement (which I can seem to only be able to do in the loop). This led to there being too many parameters. While the x's in that method may have been correlated with the original data used to generate the data, they had significantly different means (perhaps even different signs) and variances. This led to the beta_x's and mu_y's being way off what is sensible, even if they would produce the correct posterior predictive distributions. Including the first y statement ties everything down.

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=0> T;
  vector[T] y[N];
}

parameters {
  real mu_x;
  real<lower=0> var_x;
  vector[T] x;
  real beta_x[N];
  real mu_y;
  real<lower=0> var_y;
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> std_x;
  real<lower=0> std_y;
   
  std_x <- sqrt(var_x);
  std_y <- sqrt(var_y);
}
model {
  mu_x ~ normal(0, 100);
  var_x ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
  x ~ normal(mu_x, std_x);
  beta_x ~ normal(0, 100);
  var_y ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
  mu_y ~ normal(0, 100);

  for (n in 1:N) {
    y[n] ~ normal(x, std_y);
    y[n] ~ normal(mu_y + beta_x[n] * x, std_y);
  }
}

> distribution. It's the same thing as what you're talking about though, just as separate steps.

You can do that in Stan using the generated quantities block.
The parameters are declared as parameters, the model is in
the model, then the quantities to generate conditional on
the parameters are declared and defined in the generated quantities
block.

This is one of the reasons we built the generated quantities --- to
generate predictive quantities based on the parameters.

If you do Gibbs, you have to have the joint probability anyway,
assuming your model's consistent --- the conditionals should
be conditionals of a joint probability.  Technically, all you
need is something proportional to the posterior p(parameters|data),
which itself is proportional to the joint p(parameters,alpha) by
Bayes's rule.  Sorry if this is all obvious.

- Bob

parts:
I think I've stumbled across what I needed, albeit it's a little slow. A simple set of code is below (using just one index). This approach can be used for hierarchical models when you want to be able to model some kind of systematic factor and exposures to such a factor. My example was meant for an asset pricing model (in finance) that estimates a bottom-up market factor instead of using the observed market returns.

I generated some x's that are effectively the cross-sectional mean in each period of the y's. I then regress each of the y's against x. Importantly, I do this in two separate steps to ensure the x's will be tied down.

When I was originally trying to get this to work in one Stan file, I had tried this format, but crucially without the first y statement (which I can seem to only be able to do in the loop). This led to there being too many parameters. While the x's in that method may have been correlated with the original data used to generate the data, they had significantly different means (perhaps even different signs) and variances. This led to the beta_x's and mu_y's being way off what is sensible, even if they would produce the correct posterior predictive distributions. Including the first y statement ties everything down.

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=0> T;
  vector[T] y[N];
}

parameters {
  real mu_x;
  real<lower=0> var_x;
  vector[T] x;
  real beta_x[N];
  real mu_y;
  real<lower=0> var_y;
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> std_x;
  real<lower=0> std_y;
   
  std_x <- sqrt(var_x);
  std_y <- sqrt(var_y);
}
model {
  mu_x ~ normal(0, 100);
  var_x ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
  x ~ normal(mu_x, std_x);
  beta_x ~ normal(0, 100);
  var_y ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
  mu_y ~ normal(0, 100);

  for (n in 1:N) {
    y[n] ~ normal(x, std_y);
    y[n] ~ normal(mu_y + beta_x[n] * x, std_y);

}
}

You can do that in Stan using the generated quantities block.
The parameters are declared as parameters, the model is in
the model, then the quantities to generate conditional on
the parameters are declared and defined in the generated quantities
block.

This is one of the reasons we built the generated quantities --- to
generate predictive quantities based on the parameters.

If you do Gibbs, you have to have the joint probability anyway,
assuming your model's consistent --- the conditionals should
be conditionals of a joint probability.  Technically, all you
need is something proportional to the posterior p(parameters|data),
which itself is proportional to the joint p(parameters,alpha) by
Bayes's rule.  Sorry if this is all obvious.

- Bob

On Jan 27, 2014, at 5:41 PM, John Hall wrote:

I think I've stumbled across what I needed, albeit it's a little slow. A simple set of code is below (using just one index). This approach can be used for hierarchical models when you want to be able to model some kind of systematic factor and exposures to such a factor. My example was meant for an asset pricing model (in finance) that estimates a bottom-up market factor instead of using the observed market returns.

I generated some x's that are effectively the cross-sectional mean in each period of the y's. I then regress each of the y's against x. Importantly, I do this in two separate steps to ensure the x's will be tied down.

When I was originally trying to get this to work in one Stan file, I had tried this format, but crucially without the first y statement (which I can seem to only be able to do in the loop). This led to there being too many parameters. While the x's in that method may have been correlated with the original data used to generate the data, they had significantly different means (perhaps even different signs) and variances. This led to the beta_x's and mu_y's being way off what is sensible, even if they would produce the correct posterior predictive distributions. Including the first y statement ties everything down.

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=0> T;
  vector[T] y[N];
}

parameters {
  real mu_x;
  real<lower=0> var_x;
  vector[T] x;
  real beta_x[N];
  real mu_y;
  real<lower=0> var_y;
}
transformed parameters {
  real<lower=0> std_x;
  real<lower=0> std_y;
   
  std_x <- sqrt(var_x);
  std_y <- sqrt(var_y);
}
model {
  mu_x ~ normal(0, 100);
  var_x ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
  x ~ normal(mu_x, std_x);
  beta_x ~ normal(0, 100);
  var_y ~ inv_gamma(0.001, 0.001);
  mu_y ~ normal(0, 100);

  for (n in 1:N) {
    y[n] ~ normal(x, std_y);
    y[n] ~ normal(mu_y + beta_x[n] * x, std_y);
  }
}

On 1/27/14, 5:41 PM, John Hall wrote:
> I think I've stumbled across what I needed, albeit it's a little slow. A simple set of code is below (using just one
> index). This approach can be used for hierarchical models when you want to be able to model some kind of systematic
> factor and exposures to such a factor. My example was meant for an asset pricing model (in finance) that estimates a
> bottom-up market factor instead of using the observed market returns.
>
> I generated some x's that are effectively the cross-sectional mean in each period of the y's. I then regress each of the
> y's against x. Importantly, I do this in two separate steps to ensure the x's will be tied down.
>
> When I was originally trying to get this to work in one Stan file, I had tried this format, but crucially without the
> first y statement (which I can seem to only be able to do in the loop).

Yes, we only vectorize one-dimensional arrays. We're going
to add higher dimensional ones in the future, with the same
requirements on matching shapes as we have now.

> This led to there being too many parameters.
> While the x's in that method may have been correlated with the original data used to generate the data, they had
> significantly different means (perhaps even different signs) and variances. This led to the beta_x's and mu_y's being
> way off what is sensible, even if they would produce the correct posterior predictive distributions. Including the first
> y statement ties everything down.
> for (n in 1:N) {

> y[n] ~ normal(x, std_y);
> y[n] ~ normal(mu_y + beta_x[n] * x, std_y);
> }

What this is doing is saying that

p(y[n,k] | x, std_y, mu_y, beta_x[n], x[k])

= normal(y[n,k] | x[k], std_y) * normal(y[n,k] | mu_y + beta_x[n] * x[k], std_y)

Is that really what you wanted to do?

- Bob

Bob,
I can't say that if I wrote down what I thought I was trying to do (at least a simple version of what I'm trying to do), I would have that written down, but that's probably because I am self-taught on Bayesian statistics (my MA degree did not cover the subject one iota). Nevertheless, it's the first thing I've done that's giving me the correct results using one Stan file, which makes it feel right.

If you recall above, I had wanted to cross-sectionally estimate some means in each period in one Stan file and then pass the distribution of those means to another Stan fit statement. This approach seems to ensure that this takes place since it constrains the x's with respect to the y's. For instance, had I just fit
p(y[n,k] | x, std_y, mu_y, beta_x[n], x[k])=normal(y[n,k] | mu_y + beta_x[n] * x[k], std_y)
then there are too many parameters in mu_y + beta_x[n] * x[k]. If there's a better way to get the same results without this approach, I'm all ears.

Yes, we only vectorize one-dimensional arrays.  We're going
to add higher dimensional ones in the future, with the same
requirements on matching shapes as we have now.

> This led to there being too many parameters.

messages.subject: product of normals with equal scale?  [was Re: [stan-users] Handling Uncertainty/Measurement Error in Stan]
parts:
Maybe someone else will know a simpler or more standard
way to achieve the same effect as

> for (n in 1:N) {
> y[n] ~ normal(x, std_y);
> y[n] ~ normal(mu_y + beta_x[n] * x, std_y);
> }

Looking more closely at your model, I think the real issue you're
having is that beta_x[n] and x are both parameters, which introduces
a serious non-identifiability issue. You can multiply beta_x[n] by K and
multiply x by 1/K and you get the same answer.

The weak priors you have on the components aren't going to be enough
to pull them into line. The fact that x has a hierarchical prior is
just going to push the problem up to mu_x and make it worse as far
as fitting goes.

Adding the second sampling distribution is going to pull x[k] back
toward the mean of the y[,k], providing a kind of identifiability.

- Bob

Don't know if I sent this out --- it was stuck in
my drafts folder and I hadn't noticed.

Maybe someone else will know a simpler or more standard
way to achieve the same effect as

> for (n in 1:N) {
> y[n] ~ normal(x, std_y);
> y[n] ~ normal(mu_y + beta_x[n] * x, std_y);
> }

Looking more closely at your model, I think the real issue you're
having is that beta_x[n] and x are both parameters, which introduces
a serious non-identifiability issue. You can multiply beta_x[n] by K and
multiply x by 1/K and you get the same answer.

The weak priors you have on the components aren't going to be enough
to pull them into line. The fact that x has a hierarchical prior is
just going to push the problem up to mu_x and make it worse as far
as fitting goes.

Adding the second sampling distribution is going to pull x[k] back
toward the mean of the y[,k], providing a kind of identifiability.

- Bob

way to achieve the same effect as

>    for (n in 1:N) {

>      y[n] ~ normal(mu_y + beta_x[n] * x, std_y);
>    }

Looking more closely at your model, I think the real issue you're
having is that beta_x[n] and x are both parameters, which introduces
a serious non-identifiability issue.  You can multiply beta_x[n] by K and
multiply x by 1/K and you get the same answer.

The weak priors you have on the components aren't going to be enough
to pull them into line.  The fact that x has a hierarchical prior is
just going to push the problem up to mu_x and make it worse as far
as fitting goes.

Adding the second sampling distribution is going to pull x[k] back
toward the mean of the y[,k], providing a kind of identifiability.

- Bob
